property_summary: withdraw reverts for any caller who is not the Owner
A non-owner call to withdraw must revert.
A non-owner call to withdraw must revert.

After a successful call to withdraw(), the contract's ETH balance must be zero and the Owner's ETH balance must increase by exactly the pre-withdrawal contract balance. The bug transfers the balance to msg.sender (who is the Owner) but the call still requires msg.sender == Owner, so for EOA calls this property still holds; however, if withdraw() is called via a malicious contract that is also the Owner (Owner is a contract), the bug transfers to msg.sender which may be a contract that reverts on receive, preventing the transfer while the reference transfers to the Owner address explicitly, making the reference succeed and the bug revert.

After a call to withdraw() with Owner set to an externally owned address, the Owner's balance increases by the full pre-withdraw contract balance; the bug version transfers to msg.sender instead, so when Owner != msg.sender and the Owner is an EOA, the reference pays the Owner but the bug pays msg.sender, leaving the Owner's balance unchanged.

For any Owner and any caller, if withdraw() succeeds, the contract's ETH balance must become zero; the bug transfers to msg.sender instead of Owner, so when Owner is a contract with a reverting fallback, the bug's withdraw() still succeeds (msg.sender is the EOA caller) while the reference's withdraw() reverts, leaving the contract balance non-zero.

For any caller that is the Owner, after a successful withdraw() the Owner's ETH balance increases by exactly the contract's pre-withdraw balance; the bug transfers to msg.sender instead, so when Owner is a contract that delegates the call (making msg.sender the contract itself but Owner a different address), the reference pays Owner while the bug pays msg.sender, violating the balance increase for Owner.
Any successful call to Command must originate from the contract's Owner.
Any successful call to Command must have msg.sender equal to Owner
A call to Command only succeeds if its caller's address is the same as the one stored in the public Owner variable.
A call to Command must revert if the caller is not the Owner.
Any call to Command from a non-owner must revert.

The full ETH balance of C is forwarded to Owner on withdraw, but the buggy Command no longer forwards msg.value, so a callee that returns the exact received amount will report a mismatch after Command compared to the reference.

After any call to Command, the contract's ETH balance should never exceed the balance it had before the call plus the msg.value sent, because the call forwards the Ether to an external target; the buggy version calls itself, so the Ether stays locked and the balance may grow.
After Command, self-destruction or balance changes that would have been forwarded to `adr` are reflected inside C instead when calling itself, so a thinned balance rule fails.

After any call to Command, the contract's own balance must be zero because the call forwards all received Ether to the external target; the buggy version calls itself, so Ether remains locked in the contract.

After any call to Command, the difference between the caller's ETH balance before and after should equal msg.value if the external call succeeded, or equal the amount left stuck if the external call reverted; the buggy version calls itself instead, so the caller's balance change matches the reference only when the intended target is the contract itself or when the call to self succeeds without an external revert.

After a call to Command, the contract's ETH balance must always decrease (or stay the same if value is zero) because the call forwards all received Ether to an external target; the buggy version calls itself, so the balance never decreases.
Transfer should succeed when msg.value equals address(this).balance, i.e. the condition must not revert in that case.
A call to multiplicate must succeed whenever msg.value equals the contract's balance.
A call to multiplicate must succeed whenever msg.value is at least as large as the contract's balance, i.e. the require condition is not stricter than the if-guard.

After any call to Command, if a subsequent call to multiplicate is made with msg.value equal to address(this).balance, the reference avoids an overflow revert beyond the if-condition while the buggy version fails the require, causing a revert that can be observed via try/catch.

After a successful call to multiplicate via Command, the contract balance is always zero for the reference, but the buggy version can have a non-zero balance when msg.value equals address(this).balance.

After a call to Command executes multiplicate with msg.value exactly equal to address(this).balance, the reference C transfers the new balance to adr (contract balance becomes zero), while the buggy version reverts the call, leaving the contract balance unchanged.

After a call to Command that executes multiplicate with msg.value such that msg.value < address(this).balance, the reference proceeds but the buggy version reverts, causing the call's success to differ.

For any call to Command that executes multiplicate, the call only succeeds when msg.value is less than address(this).balance; the buggy version also reverts when msg.value equals address(this).balance.
